chunks: Layers for high-speed signal routing. The question: Which layers should high-speed signals be routed?
Fast signals need three things: a predictable impedance, a clean return path and some isolation from neighbors.
All three come from placing the trace right next to a solid copper plane, ideally ground.
Keep each link on the same layers, and put a ground via (a plated hole down to ground) beside every signal via.
Picture a canal with banks on both sides. An inner trace between two ground planes is like that canal.
An outer trace over one plane is a channel with one bank and open air on the other side. A dead-end side channel sends waves back as echoes. That is a via stub.
The analogy is loose: signals are electric and magnetic fields, not water.
In a microstrip some field lines go through air, so propagation is faster but the line radiates and picks up more.
In a stripline every field line ends on one of the two planes, so it is shielded; propagation is slower and layer changes need vias.
Impedance: the ratio of voltage to current a fast signal sees along a trace, set by its width and its distance to the plane ("PCB layers in a stackup and their materials").
Microstrip and stripline: an outer trace over one plane, and an inner trace between two planes ("What to route on inner vs outer layers").
Via stub: the unused end of a plated hole that sticks out past the layer where the signal leaves ("Vias in high-speed traces").
Differential pair: two traces carrying opposite copies of a signal, kept together ("Differential pair and its tradeoffs").
Resonance: a frequency at which a structure rings, like a tuning fork, and swallows signal.
A through via on a 1. 6 mm board can leave a stub about 1. 4 mm long.
It resonates when it is a quarter of a wavelength long: f equals c over (4 square root of r ) ( c is the speed of light). With equals 1.
4 mm and the board material's dielectric constant r equals 4. 3 that is about 25. 8 gigahertz.
A 10 Gb/s link (ten billion bits per second) carries most of its energy below about 5 gigahertz, half its bit rate, so it is safe. At 25 Gb/s that becomes 12.
5 gigahertz, close enough to hurt. That is the whole idea.

"I route fast signals directly next to a solid ground plane, usually as an inner stripline between two grounds for long, noisy runs, or as a short microstrip on the top layer when via stubs would hurt.
I keep each interface on one layer pair, with the same via count for every bit in a bus or pair.
I avoid plane splits and adjacent signal layers with no plane between them, and at layer changes I put a ground via next to the signal via so the return current can follow."
